item.title: What Helps Young Adults Flourish?
item.description:
Happiness

What Helps Young Adults Flourish?

Achievement matters less than you might think for young adult flourishing.

Posted June 11, 2026

Key points
  • Education, work, love, and leisure all shape well-being.
  • Reaching milestones matters, but satisfaction with work, love, and life matters more.
  • Ask young adults how life feels, not just what they have achieved.

At some point in your life, you have almost certainly been asked when you will (finally) graduate, get a “real job,” get married, have a baby, or buy a house. These questions can feel cutting, even when they aren’t meant to be, because they signal that you aren’t “there” yet. You haven’t done all the things you are supposed to do.

The reality is that contemporary young people transition to adulthood slowly. It takes a long time to get the education or training needed to build a career. It takes a lot of self-exploration to feel confident and comfortable building a life with another person, becoming a parent, or embracing singlehood. Researchers call this elongated path to adulthood emerging adulthood—a developmental period between ages 18 and 29 when many people lean into identity exploration, getting an education, and exploring life’s possibilities. Emerging adulthood is a time of instability and transition because people are often in progress on some of the most important building blocks of adult life: education, work, and love.

For a long time, scholars have approached studying the transition to adulthood as a series of developmental milestones to hit. They look for people to become financially independent, become employed full-time, finish their education, and start a family. Once all those boxes are ticked, the assumption is that a person will have made a successful transition to adulthood.

The problem is that this approach doesn’t account for whether a person feels good about their job, relationship, or educational outcomes. It only matters whether they have completed the task or not.

In a recent study with Jonathon Beckmeyer and Cindy Hartman, we tried to address this problem by exploring whether a person’s feelings about different areas of their lives mattered more or less than whether they had achieved milestones in that domain. Using data from 857 young adults ages 18-35, we explored whether satisfaction with education, work, their love lives, and their leisure experiences was associated with flourishing (i.e., their overall sense of well-being).

Why Flourishing?

Social scientists commonly use negative indicators of well-being like anxiety, depression, or loneliness as outcome variables in their studies. In some ways, this approach is important because it helps us identify people most at risk of problems in the hopes of developing appropriate supports for them.

However, negative measures don’t tell the whole story about well-being. A person can lack indicators for depression or anxiety and still be struggling or stagnant. Flourishing measures the extent to which people feel good about their lives and feel a sense of purpose and optimism about the future. The scale we used asks questions like: Do you feel respected? Do you contribute to the happiness of others? Do you feel like a good person? We used flourishing as our outcome because we believe it is critical to understanding whether someone has made a successful transition to adulthood.

What Promotes Flourishing?

Participants were flourishing when they felt good about their experiences in education, work, love, and leisure. These subjective assessments of satisfaction mattered more than whether they had accomplished objective markers of success in each area of their lives. These findings were consistent across men and women and across ages.

Did achieving a task make young people feel subjectively better about it? Yes. That means that it is important to continue building systems that help young people reach their goals. However, even if a task is not finished yet, it can still be a meaningful part of flourishing. Although we did not include it specifically in this study, we think progress matters. Moving toward a goal likely yields some benefits, and then completing a task boosts satisfaction even more.

Key Takeaways

In achievement-oriented cultures, it can be easy to overlook how something feels in favor of the results or outcomes it produces. For young people working toward their goals, stopping to assess whether they are satisfied and find meaning in work, education, love, and leisure is an important part of satisfaction and well-being.

For people navigating the delicate transition of parenting young adult children, it may be helpful to prioritize asking them about how a certain part of their life is going rather than when they will graduate, get a job, or get married.

Reaching goals matters, but feeling good about where you are matters more.

item.title: How Couples Can Survive Romantic Betrayal
item.description:
Infidelity

How Couples Can Survive Romantic Betrayal

After a breach of trust, there is a path forward.

Posted June 11, 2026

Key points
  • Examples of romantic betrayals include infidelity, dishonesty, and lack of emotional support.
  • The chances of a relationship surviving betrayal depend on the perpetrator's perspective.
  • Betrayal can cause relational damage as well as reputational damage.

There is nothing as special, even magical, about the warm glow of new romance. The period of time when partners are getting to know more about each other every day. As time goes by and trust is solidified, both parties become increasingly invested in the relationship, envisioning a bright future together. Many couples experience exactly that over the course of a lifetime, from walking down the aisle to walking into the sunset decades later. Other couples, however, are not that lucky. Somewhere along the line, one or both spouses break their vows.

The most commonly cited form of romantic betrayal is infidelity, which may be physical or emotional, an intentional strategic act, or an impulsive decision made under the influence of an intoxicant. The ability to recover from the event, however, often depends on the perspective of the perpetrator. Research explains.

Source: Sunrise / Pixabay

Harnessing the Reasons for Heartbreak

Romantic betrayal is experienced every day by partners around the globe from every demographic background. While many studies have focused on the betrayed “innocent” partner, recent research has focused on the betrayer, seeking to understand how betrayer motivation predicts relational dissolution or restoration.

F. Lalot et al. (2026) studied the reasons for betrayal in a piece entitled “The Things We Do to Each Other.”[i] They defined betrayal as “a voluntary violation of mutually known pivotal expectations of the trustor by the trusted party (trustee), which has the potential to threaten the well-being of the trustor.” They collected and analyzed more than 1100 betrayal narratives from the point of view of the relationship betrayer from university students and community participants across five countries and three languages: France, Germany, Switzerland, the United States, and the United Kingdom. In each case, Lalot et al. examined the type of betrayal, the type of relationship, and the response of the person who was betrayed, as well as the causes of disloyalty explained by the betrayer. They found a variety of different types of betrayal occurring within a range of relationships, and results including everything from forgiveness to relational dissolution to revenge.

Why Partners Stray

Lalot et al. noted several traditional examples of romantic betrayals, including infidelity, dishonesty, betraying confidences, excessive criticism, lack of emotional support, and ignoring one’s partner. They note that more recent research confirms that romantic infidelity remains the most frequently cited example of betrayal, although other reported experiences include revealing secrets, lying, manipulative behavior, gossiping, failing to assist during a time of need, and unexpectedly cutting ties.

Lalot et al. acknowledge that betrayers may incorporate a cost-benefit approach to considering betrayal, weighing what they stand to gain against potential loss. They note that costs to the perpetrator can include relational damages as well as reputational damage if others learn about the betrayal, as well as damage to the betrayer’s personal self-image and self-esteem due to the need to integrate negative behavior into personal self-concept.

Taking Responsibility Prompts Relational Repair

Regarding motivation and blame, Lalot et al. found that betrayers predominantly explained their betrayal as stemming from internal factors as opposed to blaming the innocent party or the relational dynamics. They also found that when betrayers reported strong internal attributions for betrayal, the person betrayed was more likely to have forgiven the transgression and less likely to have taken revenge. They note that this result is consistent with the notion that perpetrators who take responsibility for their actions earn more forgiveness, whereas revenge is used to send a message designed to force the betrayer to face the consequences of their betrayal, which is unnecessary if they have already taken responsibility.

As a practical matter, however, although post-betrayal confession and remorse contribute to relational repair and resilience, motive matters. A premeditated, strategic approach to securing private time with an attractive co-worker may be more emotionally devastating than a drunken one-night stand with a stranger. But both examples include additional relational hurdles, from a habit of overindulgence to poor impulse control to a compromised conscience. Nonetheless, when couples are willing to move forward, help is available to address both the betrayal and the underlying causes, to repair relational comfort and trust.

item.title: Why Your Money Story Begins Before Age 7
item.description:
Behavioral Economics

Why Your Money Story Begins Before Age 7

A childhood memory of one holiday season, and why this early money memory lingers.

Posted June 11, 2026

Key points
  • Research suggests the cognitive foundations for financial habits are largely laid by around age 7.
  • Parental silence around money predicts worse credit-card and financial behavior in adult children.
  • Recognizing your first money memory is one of the simplest starting points for rewriting the story.

In my last post, I wrote about a question my 8-year-old, Sam, asked me one morning at the breakfast table. Today, I want to look in the other direction, to my own childhood, and what that has to do with the financial realities today.

We were two children, one employed adult, and Christmas was coming. My parents were managing, but only just, and they had gradually begun to lower expectations, perhaps their own as well.

So they told their 5-year-old daughter, well in advance, that Santa Claus had received so many letters that winter that he had run out of presents. Santa is generous, they explained, but Santa is not bottomless. Everybody knew, of course, that Santa did not actually manufacture the gifts. He bought them, like anyone else.

For a 5-year-old, this was a disaster.

But children often have an unnerving ability to solve problems before the adults around them notice. I went to my room, found old toys, and wrapped them carefully. One for my mother, one for my father, one for each of my grandparents, and some for myself and my brother. By the morning, I had become, in my own mind, the hero of Christmas. There would be presents under the tree. There would be the best part of Christmas, the opening. I had solved the first money problem of my life and brought joy to my family.

This is my first memory of money.

The ending was happier than I expected. Santa, it turned out, had found gifts for the young family after all. The old toys were quietly returned to my bedroom, and the matter was never mentioned again.

And yet, that Christmas has stayed with me my whole life. It is a memory about adapting to something a child has a hard time understanding. It is also a memory about something common, the kind of relative scarcity and insecurity that exists in many families, unremarkable incidents that carry the weight of heavy emotions.

The Story I Did Not Know I Had

That memory, and the dozens that followed, quietly built a way of thinking I never noticed I had. I came to believe that whether we had plenty of money or just about enough, we would manage, and our problems would be temporary. I also came to believe that the lack of money should be discussed as little as possible, because it was an exceptional and slightly shameful situation that should not happen to a normal middle-income family.

For years, this unconscious way of thinking influenced countless decisions and choices. I sat in the bank applying for a mortgage. I bought a trendy financial guide. I spent money I didn’t have. I left my finances in someone else’s hands. All of this, my own story about money, had started very early, long before I had the words for it.

What Behavioral Science Says About Early Money Learning

Behavioral scientists Sue Bingham and David Whitebread of the University of Cambridge reviewed the evidence on how children develop a relationship with money. Their 2013 report for the United Kingdom’s Money Advice Service concluded that the cognitive and metacognitive foundations of later financial behavior, things like self-control, working memory, and the ability to apply rules of money management, are typically in place by around age 7 (Whitebread and Bingham, 2013). By the time formal financial education begins in school, much of the underlying architecture is already there.

Financial psychologists have given these patterns a name. Brad and Ted Klontz, drawing on two decades of clinical work and testing the framework empirically in a sample of 422 adults, describe them as money scripts, which are simply unconscious beliefs about money, usually formed in childhood, driving adult financial behavior (Klontz, Britt, Mentzer, and Klontz, 2011). Klontz hypothesizes that these scripts often pass down through families, like recipes nobody wrote out. They feel like common sense, not like beliefs. And they steer some of our most consequential adult choices: whether we open the bill or let it sit on the counter, whether we celebrate a raise or feel quietly guilty about it, whether we tell our partner about a purchase or smuggle it home in an old cloth bag.

What predicts a child carrying harmful scripts into adulthood is not, as one might expect, the family’s debt or income. In a study of 173 college students, parents’ own struggles with debt did not significantly predict their children’s debt levels, but having parents who avoided talking about finances did predict problematic credit-card use as young adults (Norvilitis and MacLean, 2010). The silence matters more than we think.

An Inheritance, Not a Destiny

This is not a counsel of despair. We might say that the childhood money story is more of an inheritance than destiny, and the first step in rewriting the story is recognizing that we have one. After all, we all do.

So here is the question I would like to leave with you, the same one I had to sit with myself:

What is your first memory of money?

Sit with whatever comes up. Notice whether the memory is about lack or about plenty, about silence or about openness, about shame or about pride. Notice the small details, what you were wearing, who was in the room, what was said, and what was not said. That memory may still be active, helping to mould your financial life today. The good news is that once you begin to recognise the memorable moment, you can begin to choose what to do with it.

Adapted from Money Values: How to Be Financially Mindful (Prometheus, 2026).

item.title: Dark Tetrad: A Set of Traits and a Relational Strategy
item.description:
Dark Tetrad

Dark Tetrad: A Set of Traits and a Relational Strategy

Why Dark Tetrad traits might begin to look adaptive to some when they're not.

Posted June 11, 2026

Key points
  • Dark Tetrad traits (narcissism, psychopathy, Machiavellianism, and sadism) can also be a relational strategy.
  • The behaviors associated with the Dark Tetrad can serve as a defense against vulnerability and helplessness.
  • In a culture of keyboard warriors and uncivil leaders, Dark Tetrad behaviors may seem adaptive, but are not.

I recently published a study that found that people who really like political leaders who are uncivil, who frequently don’t have their facts straight, and who don't have evidence on their side score highly on Dark Triad characteristics (Killian, 2025). As a quick review, Dark Triad traits are narcissism—grandiosity, “I’m the center of the universe,” sensitivity to criticism; Machiavellianism—manipulative, purely transactional in relationships; and psychopathy—low empathy, low to no remorse, detached. The fourth factor in the Dark Tetrad is sadism (i.e., deriving pleasure from cruelty to others).

Estrangement Culture

These four characteristics exist on a spectrum, and it is important to keep in mind that most people who display facets of them may not be diagnosable. But psychologist Joshua Coleman (2026) points out how increasingly rewarded these traits are nowadays, especially in online interactions where anonymity and a lack of consequences for posting insults and abuse make for an “open season” for keyboard warriors. Most are by now familiar with the term cancel culture. Coleman drills down on estrangement culture. He holds that beneath many contemporary relationship narratives is a fantasy of invulnerability, represented by the following mantras: “I owe no one access to me. I owe no one explanations. I owe no one repair. If you hurt me, disappoint me, frustrate me, or fail to affirm me, I can exile you without guilt.”

Folks who score high on Dark Tetrad traits and low on critical thinking dispositions (see Killian, 2024, 2025) may tend to reduce or flatten people and relationships into rigid categories and moralistic binaries (Coleman, 2026). We see a cognitive style (need for closure) and behaviors (snap judgments) organized around either/or rigid dichotomies, and a rush to judge and to condemn. The ongoing narrative becomes “I am the hero of this story, and you necessarily are the villain.”

When this defense mechanism is over-utilized, empathy and compassion tend to collapse, as others do not deserve consideration or gentleness. When this occurs, ordinary human foibles and frailties begin to be viewed with disdain and contempt. Most distressing is the normalization of relational strategies that look increasingly Dark-Tetrad-adjacent while being framed as “healthy.” Coleman (2026) provides the following examples:

  • Strategic withdrawal rather than engaging in a difficult dialogue (quitting so you don't have to do something hard)
  • Emotional withholding as power ("I’ll punish you by not speaking to you" or dismissing you altogether)
  • Viewing vulnerability (and even the act of changing one’s mind in the face of new evidence) as weakness
  • Seeing attachment itself as a “dangerous dependency”

Why Dark Tetrad Is an Appealing Strategy for Some

A Dark Tetrad relational strategy can seem like the way to go when people seek protection from vulnerability and helplessness. If I stay detached, I can’t be abandoned. If I stay superior, I can’t feel shame. If I stay strategic, I never have to risk genuine need (Coleman, 2026). However, couple and family life inevitably requires tolerating disappointments, misunderstandings, and people who are less than perfect over long periods of time. Here are some alternative mantras (Coleman, 2026): What you said hurt me, and I still love you. You may have failed me, but I still see and affirm your humanity. I needed more from you and your own wounds, and fears got in the way. I can protect myself without having to erase you.

These represent actual psychological and relational health. But they are far more difficult than simple exile. And refusing to categorize people and dismiss them is also much harder than simply splitting people into binaries like good and bad, patriotic and treasonous, etc. In contemporary culture and on social media platforms like X and Truth Social, Dark Tetrad characteristics and behaviors become normalized and begin to stop looking cruel and unusual. In those harsh realms, the Dark Tetrad strategy begins to look adaptive.

Helping professionals and intimate partners can take it upon themselves to assess to what degree and frequency and in what contexts Dark Tetrad traits, behaviors, and strategy are evidenced in their clients and partners and challenge the idea that this strategy is either healthy or relationship sustaining. Because it’s not. Abuse is not protection. Cruelty is not kindness. And just because you’re only out for “number one” doesn’t mean everybody else shares that perspective and value system.

item.title: Social Connections, Not Social Media, Will Help Young Men
item.description:
Gender

Social Connections, Not Social Media, Will Help Young Men

Effective models for young men to engage with themselves and others.

Posted June 11, 2026

Key points
  • Looksmaxxing exploits young men's insecurities, and doesn't lead to true connection or happiness.
  • Positive real-life social connections, not online advice, boost young men's confidence and well-being.
  • Overcoming anxiety and seeking real-world growth is key to fighting isolation among young men.

To paraphrase an internet meme, “Men used to go to war; now they livestream.” Sadly, some of those streamers are actively undermining positive images of what it means to be a man today. For instance, spectacularly popular “looksmaxxers” like Clavicular and Androgenic encourage young men to pursue any means necessary to look good: Their advice to look better and attract women has included taking meth to lose weight and hitting their jaws with hammers to reshape their jawline. It’s easy to dismiss their advice and behavior as extremism meant to attract clicks and make them money. But their popularity also suggests that young men today are desperately seeking ways to feel confident and connected in a fragmented world.

Unfortunately, this current focus on looksmaxxing is not going to make young men happy, connected, and successful. Instead, young men need better guidance in finding social acceptance and self-confidence.

I’ve researched body image and its impact on well-being for decades. In some ways, the looksmaxxing trend is the logical extension of pressures women have felt. In the 1980s and earlier, women’s fashion featured rail-thin models and pushed women toward eating disorders to try to attain what was being presented as the ideal physique. As with lookssmaxing, those trends sold an impossible ideal—and one that wasn’t even accurate. Research throughout the 1980s showed that women consistently believed that men preferred women who were much thinner than those men actually preferred.

Focusing on “perfecting” looks for both genders exploits our natural insecurities about whether people will accept us as we are. For decades, mass media campaigns targeted women and exploited social pressures to make them feel badly about themselves, to sell products, from butt- or thigh-toning exercise equipment to ephedrine, a stimulant used to facilitate weight loss that caused cardiac events and deaths in users. Today’s looksmaxxers are exploiting young men’s insecurities to draw viewers, increase clicks, and generate ad revenue.

Why Are Young Men Falling for This Now?

The popularity of looksmazing influencers suggests that young men are clearly seeking out something. Men are feeling alone; a recent Gallup poll revealed that more than a quarter of US young men report feeling lonely, much higher than US women (18 percent) and other men aged 35-54 (15 percent). But screen time alone is not the reason for this feeling of isolation; surveys like Gallup's indicate that teen girls have more daily screen time than teen boys.

The solution, though, can’t be found by consuming looksmaxxing content or other streams stressing how to be a man, like the “incel” movement that bashes women. Instead, the solution lies in teaching young men how to build real-world connections. These three steps can help do just that.

First, we can switch up the content and promote more positive messages that advance self-development and personal growth. If people are interested in “looksmaxxing,” Layne Norton, a researcher and powerlifter, has a podcast on effective workouts and supplements. Young Blood, a podcast hosted by Cal MacPherson, includes guests discussing topics related to men’s mental health and topics like losing a parent, managing gambling addictions, and loneliness–all of which feature real insights and not pre-fab or cookie-cutter pseudo-solutions.

Existing interests and hobbies can also be built up to be more social. If a person loves gaming, there are many ways to develop connections with others while gaming. Colleges and universities have gaming clubs that young people can join and share their interests with others in the real world, and maybe build relationships that go beyond gaming.

Encouraging Real-World Growth

Finally, the best ways to develop and grow probably are not found while consuming online content. Young men, feeling increasingly isolated in the world, need to break through the barriers of anxiety and anxiousness to try new things. That doesn’t mean it’s easy, and building real-world connections to other people requires accepting some risks.

For instance, it’s a lot easier and more comfortable to watch streamers talk about quick fixes than to go to the gym or exercise in general. Not just because sweating it out is hard, but also because young people often feel out of place or anxious at the gym, according to researchers at the University of Lethbridge in Canada. They found that young people are concerned about their ability to exercise and about other people's judgments. But the former can be helped by the thousands of videos online demonstrating exercise form, and the latter by self-development to reduce our worries about what other people think (I recommend reading the classic book How to Stubbornly Refuse to Make Yourself Miserable About Anything, Yes Anything, by Albert Ellis).

Some people argue that young men already have plenty of advantages and resources online and off. That may be true, but those resources don’t seem to be taking. Young men are feeling isolated and threatened, and are turning to online snake oil salesmen for solutions.

Instead, we need to build stronger, healthier frameworks that empower young men to connect authentically with themselves and others. Part of this might start with meeting some of them where they are, and adapting habits like content consumption or gaming to be more social and self-enhancing. And a part of this has to be men manning up, not by reshaping their jawlines, but by learning to face challenges like anxiety and isolation through growth and development of their own interests and passions. In the end, we need to help young men focus less on maxxing their looks and more on maxxing their positive social connections and self-confidence.

item.title: What Did All Enlightenment Thinkers Have In Common?
item.description:
Philosophy

What Did All Enlightenment Thinkers Have In Common?

Kant’s legacy: free speech and individual rights.

Posted June 11, 2026

Key points
  • In a famous essay, Kant set out to define the Enlightenment.
  • For all their differences, the Enlightenment thinkers had this one thing in common: faith in reason.
  • Kant viewed perpetual peace as the culmination of the Enlightenment ideal.
Immanuel Kant at the age of 44, by Johann Gottlieb Becker.
Source: Wikimedia Commons/Johann Gottlieb Becker/Public Domain.

In 1783, two years after the publication of his masterpiece, The Critique of Pure Reason, the 59-year-old Immanuel Kant could finally afford to buy himself a house. A wall had to be knocked down to create a lecture room, since lectures in those days were not held on university premises but in private rooms, often in the lecturer’s lodgings.

A year after purchasing his house, Kant published an essay in response to a question posed by the Revered Johann Zöllner in a German periodical. The reactionary reverend had asked against the liberals: “What is enlightenment? This question, which is almost as important as what is truth, should be answered before one begins to enlighten! And still I have never found it answered!”

Kant’s Famous Essay: What is Enlightenment?

Kant published his response, entitled, Answer to the Question: What is Enlightenment, in his preferred outlet, the Berlin Monthly. The short, thousand-word piece remains widely read, and is especially remembered for its first paragraph:

Enlightenment is man’s emergence from his self-imposed immaturity. Immaturity is the inability to use one’s understanding without guidance from another. This immaturity is self-imposed when its cause lies not in lack of understanding, but in lack of resolve and courage to use it without guidance from another. Sapere aude [Dare to Know! Dare to be Wise!] “Have the courage to use your own understanding!”—that is the motto of enlightenment.

Kant goes on to advance free speech, “the freedom to use reason publicly in all matters”, as the prerequisite of progress and enlightenment, and praises his king, Frederick the Great, “a shining example”, for having granted it to him and other Prussian subjects.

What All Enlightenment Thinkers Had in Common

In 1754, following the success of his First Discourse and his one-act opera, Le Devin du village, Jean-Jacques Rousseau returned to Geneva and converted back from Catholicism to Calvinism (a form of Protestantism). But in private, he embraced a personal, natural religion, or “religion of the heart,” which, together with his belief in the corrupting influence of civilization, set him apart from other Enlightenment thinkers such as Diderot and Voltaire, who championed reason, progress, and atheism.

For all their deep differences, what united the proponents of the Enlightenment (Aufklärung in German, les Lumières in French), from Hume and Voltaire to Kant and Rousseau, was a faith in reason as the source of knowledge and authority, and a commitment to applying reason to challenge superstition, dogma, and absolute authority and achieve human progress.

The Impact of the Enlightenment on Modern Democracy

Enlightenment concepts and principles such as government by consent, the separation of church and state, and individual rights and freedoms including religious freedom and free speech are at the heart of the modern democracies that, much better than any other system of government, guarantee our security, liberty, and prosperity—and, dare I say, dignity.

In his essay, Idea for a Universal History with a Cosmopolitan Purpose, published in the same year as What is Enlightenment, Kant argues that history is a teleological process (a process with an end or goal) tending to the full expression of human rationality and morality, manifested by the establishment of a perfectly just and stable constitution within states (initially, European states), which come together to form a federation, or league of nations, to secure universal individual freedoms and perpetual peace. In 1795, Kant followed up his essay with a much more substantial book entitled, Toward Perpetual Peace: A Philosophical Sketch.

Here are a few snippets:

It is not without cause that men feel the burden of their existence, though they are themselves the cause of those burdens.

Without man and his potential for moral progress, the whole of reality would be a mere wilderness, a thing in vain, and have no final purpose.

A league of a special sort must... be established, one that we can call a league of peace, which will be distinguished from a treaty of peace because the latter seeks merely to stop one war, while the former seeks to end all wars forever.

Thus, although better known for his metaphysics, epistemology, and ethics, Kant is sometimes regarded as the intellectual father of both the European Union and the United Nations, and, more generally, of the rules-based international order.

It's fair to say, he merited the house that he bought, which, ironically, was bombed and destroyed in the Second World War.

Neel Burton is the author of the newly published The German Greeks: German Philosophy and the German Philosophers.

item.title: Mechanisms and Mitigations of Social Media’s Socially Isolating Effects
item.description:
Social Networking

Mechanisms and Mitigations of Social Media’s Socially Isolating Effects

How digital technology makes us lonely, and what to do about it.

Posted June 11, 2026

Key points
  • Mindful technology use reinforces attentiveness to the real world and strengthen interpersonal trust.
  • Some users may benefit from the connection opportunities that social media provides.
  • Social comparison on curated feeds fuels inadequacy, leading to further isolation.

Clearly, for many, social media is deeply embedded in their everyday lives, shaping how they initiate, maintain, and interpret their interpersonal relationships. Although such digital platforms offer some opportunities for connection, communication, and community-building, much research highlights their potential to produce social isolation. Rather than strengthening social bonds, excessive or maladaptive social media use actually undermines relationship quality, diminishes emotional intimacy, and fosters a sense of social disconnection—perhaps even alienation. However, there are practical strategies that can mitigate this digital isolation and promote healthier, more meaningful interpersonal engagement.

The concept of "alone together," described by Sherry Turkle,1 illustrates how social media can undermine relationship quality. Individuals may be physically present with others but remain mentally focused on their devices, leading to superficial engagement and emotional distance. Over time, this divided attention weakens even the closest of relationships.2 A practical solution is to adopt mindful technology use. This might include placing phones out of reach during conversations, actively listening without distractions, and prioritising quality interaction over multi-tasking. Such habits reinforce attentiveness to the real world and strengthen interpersonal trust.

Displacement of Face-to-Face Interaction

A key process through which social media contributes to social isolation is the displacement of face-to-face interaction.3 Interpersonal relationships rely on nuanced, in-person exchanges that convey emotional depth through tone, body language, and physical presence.4 Digital communication, by contrast, relies heavily on curated text, edited images, and brief interactions that lack these richer communicative cues—and, in fact, mimic the social style of a psychopath, and there is plenty of advice about how to deal with such interactions.5

As time spent online increases, opportunities for meaningful in-person interactions decline—time is not an infinite commodity. This shift can weaken real relational bonds, as a quick digital exchange often substitutes for deeper social conversations.2,3 To reduce this isolating effect, individuals can adopt intentional behaviours, such as scheduling regular in-person meetings, prioritising device-free time with others, and setting boundaries around screen use—particularly during meals or social gatherings. If you must use your device, then use it to supplement, rather than substitute, real-world communication. For example, messaging platforms can be used to arrange in-person activities, rather than to replace them.6

Social Comparison

Another important factor in weakening social bonds is social comparison7—a particular favourite of the ineffective, but power-crazed manager.8 Social media platforms encourage the presentation of idealised versions of lives, showcasing achievements and positive experiences, while omitting any difficulties (the latter is probably wise, by the way). Exposure to these heavily curated portrayals can lead others viewing them to feel inadequate or excluded. In turn, this feeling may generalise throughout the person’s life and prompt withdrawal from real-world relationships.7 Over time, this cycle reinforces isolation, as individuals become less inclined to engage socially. An effective strategy to counter this (apart from just not interacting with the digital device) is to develop a critical awareness of online content—remind yourself that what you see is selective, edited, and possibly untrue—think of how you perceive a politician’s speech.

In fact, the very design of social media platforms contributes to creating isolation. Algorithms often prioritise content that provokes emotional responses, encouraging prolonged engagement, but potentially increasing anxiety or dissatisfaction.9 Users may become preoccupied with online validation, such as likes or comments, which can distort their sense of self-worth and strain relationships. To mitigate this, strategies such as disabling notifications, limiting daily usage, or setting specific times for social media engagement can help reduce compulsive checking behaviours. These approaches allow individuals to regain control over their time and attention, creating more space for offline interactions.

Passive Consumption

Patterns of social media use generated by its design matter for social relationships. Passive consumption—scrolling without interacting—is linked to increased feelings of loneliness,10 although the situation may not be that much better for active use.10 To counteract passive use, individuals can shift toward more purposeful engagement, such as meaningful conversations, participating in supportive online communities, or sharing content that invites genuine dialogue. At the same time, balancing this with offline activities, such as joining clubs, volunteering, or engaging in hobbies, can diversify social experiences and reduce reliance on digital interaction.

However, it is important to recognise individual differences in all of this. Some users, particularly those who already feel socially isolated offline, may benefit from the connection opportunities that social media provides.6 That said, they may benefit more from almost anything, within reason. For these individuals, a goal may not be to eliminate social media use, but to integrate it to support broader social engagement. Strategies, such as using online platforms to find local events, build interest-based communities, or maintain long-distance relationships, can transform social media into a tool for connection, rather than isolation.

Conclusion

While social media has the potential for enhanced communication, its excessive or unbalanced use can lead to significant isolation. Factors such as reduced face-to-face interaction, social comparison, algorithm-driven engagement, and social displacement all contribute to this effect. These challenges are not insurmountable. Adopting intentional strategies, like prioritising offline interaction, managing screentime, engaging more actively and mindfully online, and critically evaluating digital content, can reduce the isolating effects of social media. The question is: Why do all of this, when the easiest thing is to turn off your social media and go and do something more interesting instead? Nobody would tell the alcoholic at death’s door to keep drinking the gut rot that is killing them, but just to have some milk beforehand to mitigate the effects.

item.title: Why Is One Twin Favored Over the Other?
item.description:
Understanding Twins

Why Is One Twin Favored Over the Other?

The long-term effects of assigning roles to siblings and twins.

Posted June 11, 2026

Key points
  • Labeling twins as opposites harms their self-esteem and identity development.
  • Comparing twins intensifies rivalry and may fuel abuse or academic struggles.
  • Encouraging individuality helps each twin build a healthy, distinct identity.
Source: Halfpoint/Istockphoto

It is difficult to tell twins apart, especially identical twins, because they look so similar and their behaviors are also very much alike. Learning to see the real differences between twins can be extremely difficult for new parents, who are not aware of the difficulty twins may have separating from each other. It is so very critical that gradually twins and their parents develop a singular relationship with each other as they develop individuality.

How Do Twins Develop Individual Relationships With Parents?

In other words, Twin A is more in need of comfort than Twin B, who thrives on adventure. Mother and father have to give each twin what they need. Twin A does not want to learn how to ride a roller coaster. Twin A wants to be pushed on the swing at the park by her gentle mom. Twin B gets bored on the swing and wants to try the longest slide in the park. Dad is very willing to go down the slide with her. Twin A is afraid of the slide. These differences create unique relationships between each twin and their parents. Differences in preferences for food, activities, and friendships begin to establish different parent-child relationships that are crucial to develop unique aspects of each child's identity.

There is much curiosity concerning why parents favor one twin over the other. It is related to the labeling of twins as opposites, as the good twin and the bad twin. Most likely, parents see labeling as an easy way to differentiate twins superficially. Most twins who have been split between “good” and “bad” are understandably upset. Twins who are treated as opposites of one another and know of my research and writing on twin identity always ask me, “Why did this happen? Is it my fault? Was I constantly causing trouble?”

I can find no answer to labelling twins as opposites that makes any sense or that reflects serious thought that went into the decision. In reality, like many twins I have worked with, I was the bad twin and my sister was the good twin for no known reason or no good reason. It seems like it just happens in the parents’ attempt to relate to each child as their own person. Unfortunately, favoring one twin is an extremely detrimental way to develop identity differences between twins and creates long-term problems. Or said in a different way; “Why is it acceptable to call one twin the good one and the other twin the bad one?” Or various other opposite labels, such as the “smart” twin and the “slow” twin. The “outgoing” twin and the “withdrawn” twin are also common ways that are ultimately harmful to natural and normal identity development for both of the twin pair.

Why Are Opposite Labels Harmful to Twins’ Identity?

Parents have to find real differences between their children because opposite labels will undermine the child’s sense of self and self-esteem. Opposite labels are statements like “Twin A is a better reader” and “Twin B is more social and makes friends for the pair.” This splitting aspect of personal identity makes learning harder and competition between the twins much stronger, and can contribute to intense physical and verbal abuse later on, years and decades later, as the labels persist.

There are other aspects of labeling that are very dangerous to identity development. Often one twin takes over one skill like reading and the other twin takes over another skill like math or history. Twin sharing of learning creates very serious problems. A humorous example comes from a parent of twins in London who called to ask if one of her twins had neurological issues. This child was in school and her twin sister was home sick in bed. The twin at school could not read a word and the teachers thought that she was suffering from a neurological problem. The twin at home was doing all of her homework easily and well. After much deliberation with the parents it became clear to me that the non-reading twin was always copying her sister and had not learned to read. The parents began reading with the twin that lagged behind and she no longer appeared to have a neurological issue.

The Power of the Twin Bond

I often get questions from parents of twins who ask me about the best way to raise twins. In general, developing an understanding of each child and not comparing them is the most effective way to raise twins to get along and learn to talk to one another. I realize that knowing twins for who they really are and not comparing them is easier said than done. And when you add in the power of the twin bond to complicate objective differences you can be sure that developing individuality is a difficult and ongoing problem.

Twins easily imitate each other for comfort and for fun. Some twins think that it is funny to trick people or confuse them. I know that my sister and I did this to others when we thought that we could get away with it. My favorite example is when we pretended we were our twin (the other twin). I was Marjorie and she was Barbara and we took our language tests in disguise. I took the French test for her and she took the Hebrew test for me. And we both got A’s. It was the wrong way to handle identity confusion, but it was a very effective way to improve our academic grades. Today, a twin called to tell me she had pretended to be her sister without asking and a huge argument was restarted.

On some level it was and still is valuable to talk to non-twins about how Marjorie and I hated being compared. Actually I think that non-twins really do not understand how painful comparison was and is. But at least it helped my sister, and other twins I have consulted with, to learn about the pitfalls and danger of comparing twins. Being a twin was and still is very hard and not as much fun as people imagine.

How Can Twins Develop Their Own Individuality?

Knowing who you are in relationship to your sister or brother is essential. For example, “My twin sister Amy loves potato chips and I don’t like them at all. She likes to wear jeans to school and I would never wear jeans to school because I think it is sloppy looking. Amy hangs out with the popular girls and I hang out with the smart girls. Amy likes to date and I like to read. We are very different in our interests and friendships.”

Obviously there are different and maybe more serious ways that twins are different, which develop as they grow and mature. By avoiding sharing clothes, friends, homework and special interests, you will accentuate the development of differences with your twin. My twin sister and I found that we liked different school subjects and wanted to study different things. She was interested in writing and poetry and I was intrigued by history. These early differences blossomed into very different but substantial careers. She became a rhetorical writing professor at Stanford and I wrote books on twin development. I studied psychology and education and followed different aspects of having a career in those fields.

As twins age it is easier to hold on to your sense of self and still find time to be a twin with your twin. By this I mean you more easily can share objects, people, and life experiences together without feeling jealous or inadequate. While twin issues with competition and comparison may continue to haunt you, it is easier to deal with them with honesty and perspective. Your sister goes to Europe for a summer holiday and you go hiking in the mountains near where you live. Both of you accept that comparing your experiences is not important.

Suggestions to Avoid Copying Your Twin

  1. Do not share friends, clothes, or accomplishments.
  2. Appreciate your differences and compliment your twin.
  3. Make family events a special time.
  4. Avoid competition and comparison.

Ways to Become More Your True Self

  1. Learn and follow your interests.
  2. Make your own friends.
  3. Spend time alone every day without your twin.

item.title: AI Isn't Replacing Us. It's Consuming Us
item.description:
Artificial Intelligence

AI Isn't Replacing Us. It's Consuming Us

Human data is becoming a technical necessity.

Posted June 11, 2026

Key points
  • AI trained on AI output eventually misperceives reality.
  • Human data isn't just valuable; it's a technical necessity.
  • The "weird, the original, and the unexpected" that gets lost from recursive AI training may be gone forever.
Source: Michell Trommler / Pixabay

Two words in a recent paper from Oxford and Cambridge stopped me cold.

The researchers were describing what happens to artificial intelligence (AI) models trained repeatedly on AI-generated data. They called it "model collapse." And in explaining the late stages, they wrote that the models "mis-perceive reality."

Two words, and a mountain of implications. This isn't a hallucination, where a model invents a fact or a false citation. Those errors tend to be discrete and correctable. What the paper describes is a system so thoroughly trained on its own output that it has lost contact with the original information. The AI is still confident and fluent but increasingly untethered from reality.

Losing the Tails of the Distribution

The paper's findings are fascinating and concerning. Each generation of AI trained on AI-generated content loses the rarest, most unusual parts of the original data first. The researchers call these "the tails of the distribution." What remains is the commonplace and expected, and the next generation trains on that. The pattern was consistent across systems—every type and every time.

The paper states plainly—and here's the key point—that genuine human-generated content will become increasingly valuable as this process continues. Not culturally or sentimentally valuable, but technically necessary. The system requires it to avoid collapse.

I wonder if we have spent years asking the wrong question. The debate has been whether human thought can survive AI, whether humans can compete with systems that, we are told, are vastly superior. This perspective assumes the dependency runs in one direction. But this paper inverts it and asks if AI can survive the disappearance of human thought.

But there's something even larger underneath that inversion.

The tails of the distribution are not just statistical curiosities. They're where new distributions come from. Newton was a tail. Einstein was a tail. Every major intellectual advance begins as an outlier, something so far from the average that no optimization process would likely have generated it. And over time and discovery, those tails gradually become the new center of gravity for everything that follows. Model collapse doesn't just lose rare information; it loses the mechanism that creates future information.

The Unrepeatable

I've written before about what I call the unrepeatable. It's the cognitive signature that belongs to a specific person, that's irreducible to any average. I meant it as a description of what AI cannot generate. The paper, in an interesting twist, suggests it's also a description of what AI cannot afford to lose. The unrepeatable isn't just personally precious. It is, in a technical sense, the resource the system is now running out of.

Every time original thought is replaced by generated thought, the ratio shifts a bit. The model consumes an output that contains less variance than the process that produced it. The change is almost invisible at first—then it compounds. Not in the way techno-optimists celebrate exponential curves that promise abundance. The same mathematics describes collapse as each generation inherits a slightly narrower version of reality.

It's time we need to recognize that human thought, at its most alive, is the friction that keeps the system from falling into a sea of average or even mediocrity. And as we've learned from this paper, it isn't just incidentally, but structurally.

Today, the conventional fear is that AI can render human cognition obsolete. However, this paper reframes this risk by revealing that human cognition is the upstream source that AI, with all its computational magic, cannot replace.
